ranking.rationale: BMI is one of the strongest and most causally proximal stable predictors of diabetes risk in BRFSS, with broad transportability across states and years. It captures metabolic risk more directly than socioeconomic, access-to-care, or domain-identifying variables, and is preferable to the coarser redundant BMI category for maximal marginal signal.

High blood pressure is a strong, clinically grounded correlate of diabetes risk that should remain predictive across states and years. It adds substantial complementary signal beyond BMI while avoiding obvious domain identifiers like state/year and being less shortcut-prone than socioeconomic or demographic variables.

Physical inactivity is a well-established, causally relevant diabetes risk factor that should remain predictive across states and years. It adds complementary lifestyle information beyond BMI and high blood pressure, while being less likely than healthcare-utilization, socioeconomic, demographic, or domain-ID variables to encode brittle distribution shifts or shortcut signals.

High cholesterol is a well-established metabolic comorbidity and risk marker for diabetes that should remain predictive across states and years. It adds complementary clinical information beyond BMI, hypertension, and physical activity, while being less tied to domain identity or socioeconomic shortcuts than features like state, year, income, education, insurance, or healthcare-utilization variables.

Routine checkup recency adds stable signal about healthcare engagement and diagnosis opportunity for diabetes beyond BMI, hypertension, activity, and high cholesterol. It is more semantically tied to case ascertainment and chronic disease management than lifestyle-noise features, while avoiding obvious domain identifiers like year/state and weaker demographic shortcuts like income or sex.

Cardiovascular disease history is a strong, semantically stable correlate of diabetes through shared metabolic risk and complications, and it adds information not already captured by BMI, hypertension, activity, high cholesterol, and checkup frequency. It is less likely than state, year, income, education, sex, or healthcare-access variables to act mainly as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut.

History of stroke is a strong, medically grounded comorbidity signal for diabetes and adds stable cardiovascular-risk information beyond hypertension, high cholesterol, BMI, inactivity, checkup frequency, and coronary disease. It is more transportable across domains than state/year or socioeconomic/demographic variables and less redundant than BMI category or smoking-detail features.

Cost-related inability to see a doctor is a robust marker of unmet care and delayed diagnosis/management that adds complementary signal beyond BMI, hypertension, activity, prior high cholesterol, checkup frequency, and cardiovascular history. It is more semantically tied to diabetes risk and detection than lifestyle micro-features here, while avoiding obvious domain identifiers like year/state and weaker demographic shortcuts like sex, income, or marital status.

Education adds broad, stable signal about diabetes risk through health literacy, long-run socioeconomic conditions, and preventive behavior, while being less domain-specific and less direct leakage than year/state or healthcare-access variables already partly captured by checkup and medcost.

Adds broadly stable signal about current health burden and diabetes complications/self-management beyond BMI, hypertension, activity, and cardiovascular history. It is more semantically tied to diabetes status across domains than demographic or domain-ID variables, and offers more marginal value than redundant BMI category or brittle access/location features.

Health care coverage adds stable signal about access to diagnosis and treatment, which is highly relevant for self-reported diabetes risk beyond BMI, hypertension, activity, education, and checkup history. It is more semantically tied to disease detection/management than lifestyle proxies, while avoiding obvious domain-ID leakage like year or state and being less shortcut-prone than income or sex.

Smoking history is a well-established, semantically stable cardiometabolic risk factor that adds complementary health-behavior signal beyond BMI, activity, hypertension, cholesterol, and healthcare-access features. It is less likely than STATE, IYEAR, INCOME, SEX, or CHECKUP-related utilization variables to act as a domain identifier or demographic shortcut, and more robust than finer smoking-status or diet variables that are noisier or more policy-dependent across domains.

Sex has strong, biologically grounded and broadly stable association with diabetes risk that is not already captured by the selected cardiometabolic and access variables. It adds complementary signal with relatively low risk of acting as a direct domain identifier compared with STATE or IYEAR, and is less shortcut-prone than socioeconomic variables like INCOME or MARITAL.

Cholesterol screening history adds stable clinical signal about cardiometabolic risk and healthcare engagement that remains predictive for diabetes across domains. It is less likely than STATE/IYEAR or socioeconomic variables to act as a domain identifier, and it contributes information not fully captured by BMI, hypertension, high cholesterol diagnosis, checkup frequency, or insurance.

Fruit intake adds plausible, domain-stable lifestyle signal for diabetes risk that is not already captured by BMI, activity, smoking, or care-access variables. It is more semantically causal and less likely to encode spurious domain identifiers or socioeconomic shortcuts than income, marital status, year, or state, and avoids redundancy with BMI category.

Vegetable intake adds a plausible, behavior-based diabetes risk signal that should generalize across domains and complements already selected BMI, activity, fruit, smoking, and cardiovascular history features. It is more semantically stable than income, marital status, year, or state, and less redundant than BMI category or smoking-frequency refinements.

Adds broadly stable health signal not yet covered: poor mental health is associated with diabetes risk and self-management across domains, while being less likely than income, marital status, state, or year to act as a domain identifier. It is also less redundant than BMI category or smoking-detail features given BMI5 and SMOKE100 are already selected.

Income adds stable marginal signal because socioeconomic status is a robust upstream determinant of diabetes risk through diet, healthcare access, stress, and living conditions, and it is not a direct domain identifier. It complements already selected health-status and behavior variables better than redundant proxies like BMI category or smoking frequency, while avoiding brittle shift features such as state or survey year.

Alcohol consumption adds plausible, semantically stable lifestyle risk information for diabetes that is not already captured by the selected set. It is more likely to generalize across domains than survey year/state, less shortcut-prone than marital status, and less redundant than BMI category or smoking-frequency variants given BMI5 and SMOKE100 are already included.

Binge drinking adds a health-behavior signal linked to diabetes risk that is more stable across domains than survey year or state and less redundant than BMI category or smoking-frequency refinements given BMI5 and SMOKE100 are already selected. It is also less likely to act primarily as a demographic or domain identifier than marital status.

Marital status adds some stable, indirect signal through household structure, stress, and age-linked life patterns, while being less domain-specific than survey year or state and less redundant than BMI category or smoking-frequency details given BMI5 and SMOKE100 are already selected.

Current smoking intensity adds some stable health-behavior signal beyond ever-smoked status, while the other candidates are less suitable: BMI category is largely redundant with continuous BMI, and survey year/state are strong domain identifiers that risk shortcutting OOD splits.

BMI category adds a robust nonlinear obesity signal closely tied to diabetes risk and is more likely to generalize across domains than survey year or state, which primarily encode domain identity and spurious shifts. Although partly redundant with continuous BMI, it can still improve stability by capturing threshold effects.

Survey year may add limited stable signal via secular diabetes prevalence and care trends, while state is a strong domain identifier likely to hurt OOD generalization. Between the two remaining options, year has the higher marginal value and lower shortcut risk.

Only remaining candidate, but it should be strongly downweighted: state mainly encodes domain/location effects, policy and sampling differences, and demographic composition rather than a stable causal signal for diabetes risk, so its marginal out-of-distribution value is low and potentially harmful.
